{"slug": "frontend-vs-backend-explained-simply", "title": "Frontend vs Backend, Explained Simply (2026 Guide)", "metaTitle": "Frontend vs Backend, Explained Simply (2026 Guide)", "metaDescription": "Frontend vs backend, explained with a real login form example. Learn what each layer does, where they meet, and why the distinction matters when you build.", "targetKeyword": "frontend vs backend, explained simply", "category": "Glossary", "bodyHtml": "

If you have ever heard a developer say something is a 'frontend problem' or a 'backend issue' and nodded along without really knowing what they meant, this page is for you. The distinction is simpler than it sounds, and once it clicks, a lot of how the web works starts making sense.

The short definitions

Frontend is everything that runs in the user's browser. It is the layout, the colors, the buttons, the animations, the form fields, and the logic that makes clicking, typing, and scrolling feel responsive. If you can see it or touch it on a screen, it is frontend.

Backend is everything that runs on a server, out of view. It handles storing and retrieving data, checking whether a password is correct, deciding what a user is allowed to see, processing payments, and sending emails. The backend does not care what a button looks like. It cares about logic, data, and rules.

The frontend is the part people experience. The backend is the part that makes what they experience trustworthy and persistent.

A concrete example: a login form, start to finish

Walk through what actually happens when someone logs into a website.

  • Frontend: The login page renders two input boxes, a 'Sign in' button, and validation that complains if you leave the password field empty. All of that is frontend code running in your browser. It looks and feels interactive, but on its own it knows nothing about whether your password is actually correct.
  • The handoff: When you click 'Sign in,' the frontend packages up your email and password and sends them to a server somewhere.
  • Backend: The server looks up your email in a database, compares the password against a securely stored hash, and if it matches, creates a session or token that proves you are logged in.
  • Back to frontend: The browser receives that confirmation and updates the screen to show your dashboard instead of the login form.

Notice that the frontend never actually verified your identity. It just collected input and displayed a result. The backend did the verifying. That split is the whole concept in miniature.

Why the distinction matters practically

This is not just trivia. It changes what you can safely build and what a given tool can actually promise you.

  • Security: Never trust logic that only lives in the frontend. A password check written only in browser code can be bypassed, because anyone can inspect or rewrite the code running on their own machine. Real validation has to happen on the backend.
  • What persists: Frontend-only apps forget everything on refresh unless a backend stores it. If you need accounts, saved data, or anything that has to survive across devices and sessions, you need a backend.
  • What a tool can honestly promise: When you evaluate any website builder or app generator, ask directly whether it produces frontend only, or frontend plus a real backend. The two are very different products, and the gap between them is exactly where broken expectations happen.

Frontend vs backend at a glance

LayerRuns whereHandlesTypical technologies
FrontendThe user's browserLayout, styling, interactivity, forms, navigationHTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Vue, Tailwind CSS
BackendA serverDatabases, authentication, business logic, APIs, paymentsNode.js, Python, databases like Postgres, server frameworks

Where Kodely fits today

Kodely currently generates real frontend applications only, which is exactly why understanding this distinction matters for setting the right expectations. When you describe a site in chat, Kodely builds an actual Vite plus React 19 plus TypeScript plus Tailwind CSS v4 app, real component files you can view and copy, not a static mockup. You get a live preview of the compiled app as it's built, and one click publishes it to a free public URL at your-name.kodely.site.

What that means honestly: Kodely today does not generate a database, authentication, or payment processing. It is a genuinely useful way to build and ship the layer users see and interact with, but if your project needs accounts, saved user data, or server-side logic, that is backend work outside Kodely's current scope. Knowing that upfront, rather than discovering it mid-project, is the entire point of this article.

Related terms worth knowing

  • API: The messenger between frontend and backend. It is a defined way for the browser code to ask the server for data or tell it to do something, like 'log this user in' or 'save this order.'
  • Database: Where a backend stores information long-term, such as user accounts, posts, or orders, so it survives after the browser closes.
  • Full-stack: A project, tool, or developer that covers both frontend and backend. A full-stack app has both the visible interface and the server-side logic and storage behind it.

FAQ

Is CSS frontend or backend?

CSS is purely frontend. It controls how things look in the browser and has no connection to servers, databases, or logic on the backend.

Can a website have a frontend without a backend?

Yes. A purely informational site, a portfolio, or a landing page can be frontend only, with no server-side logic required. The moment you need accounts, saved data, or anything dynamic tied to a specific user, you need a backend.

Do I need to know backend development to use Kodely?

No. Kodely handles generating the real frontend app for you from a plain English description. Just know that today it builds the frontend layer only, so plan backend needs like accounts or databases separately.

What is the difference between frontend and full-stack development?

Frontend development focuses only on the browser-facing layer. Full-stack development covers both the frontend and the backend, meaning the interface plus the server, database, and logic behind it.
